strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: how collaboration affects interactive qualitative coding. Comparing topic modeling, relational inference, and LLM-assisted coding is well aligned with its applied research aims.

The empirical effort is substantial: 20 researchers, 15 experiments on approximately 85,000 tweets, and a 1,200-pair human audit with double annotation and adjudication. Shared data and fixed initializations within systems improve comparability.

Separating consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and correctness provides useful complementary perspectives. Table 2 illustrates why these distinctions matter: higher cohesion can accompany higher between-theme similarity. Interviews also provide concrete observations about user control and refinement difficulties.
weaknesses: The design does not evaluate asynchronous collaboration as defined in the introduction: individual coders never consolidate their codebooks. Instead, each tool has three solo experiments and two three-person team experiments. This conflates synchrony with team size and potentially annotation effort and expertise. Participant assignment, reuse, task order, and human time budgets are insufficiently documented. The evidence supports an exploratory individual-versus-group comparison more directly than the claimed effects of collaboration modality.

The statistical significance claims are inadequately supported. Tables 1–2 report unpaired t-tests without specifying sample sizes or the independent observational unit. Each tool has only one synchronous codebook pair; theme matches and comparisons sharing codebooks are dependent. Treating these observations as independent would constitute pseudoreplication. The analysis needs to respect experiment-level dependence, report uncertainty and multiplicity handling, and distinguish descriptive differences from supported inferential conclusions.

The correctness evaluation is unclear and contains a consequential reporting inconsistency. Section 5 describes judging assigned document-theme pairs, but Figure 4 reports F1 without explaining recall or averaging. The figure shows synchronous topic modeling outperforming asynchronous at the intermediate cutoffs and tying at approximately 0.50 over all samples, contrary to the stated asynchronous advantage. Sampling weights, uncertainty, and treatment of unassigned or invalid outputs also need clarification; Table 4 reports invalid-label rates ranging from 0.7% to 16.1% for the LLM.

The automatic metrics need stronger construct validation. Maximum-similarity matching permits many-to-one correspondences and can depend on theme number and granularity, yet codebook sizes and matching aggregation are not adequately reported. LLM centroid similarities near 0.98 coexist with Jaccard similarities of only 0.14–0.17, illustrating that embedding similarity need not establish thematic agreement. Actual codebooks and human validation of theme alignments would strengthen the proposed evaluation framework.

Several conclusions exceed the tested configurations. Interaction bandwidth is not experimentally manipulated, and the systems differ in auxiliary concept information, initialization, and stopping rules. General claims about LLM reliability and scalability rest on Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct alone. One candidate prompt even invokes software-programming concepts such as a code's functionality and requirements. These results should be attributed to the evaluated implementations and dataset, rather than entire methodological families.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the promised artifact release. Missing details include the SBERT checkpoint, LLM decoding settings, selected prompt per experiment, complete codebooks, and evaluation implementation. Appendix C acknowledges missed interviews without reporting completed-interview counts or a systematic analysis procedure. The design, statistical, and correctness concerns prevent a sound Findings recommendation in the current form; reanalysis, fuller reporting, and appropriately narrowed claims could support a revised submission.
